narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 79.3% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess likely success in law school and beyond, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the two strongest factors pushing the prediction toward failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your class—far below the average of roughly the 6th decile among students who were accepted. These low rankings strongly signaled to the model that you would struggle to pass the bar.

Your family income bracket was the third most important factor, but it worked mildly in the opposite direction. Being from an upper-middle-income family slightly nudged the prediction toward success, consistent with patterns seen among many accepted applicants.

Taken together, the model concluded that your academic standing in law school outweighed the modest positive signal from your background, leading to the 79% probability of bar failure and the resulting denial.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses, consider bar-prep programs that target students with similar profiles, or explore schools and pathways with different success metrics. Improving your class ranking would have the largest impact on future predictions. (218 words)
